questions.topic: Style: word choice, syntax and tone
questions.passage: (1) Last spring, the teens at the Eastside Branch Library asked for a “quiet hour” on Thursday afternoons, but the first three sessions were anything but quiet. (2) Phones buzzed against tables, group chats lit up, and the same handful of students who had requested silence spent most of the hour explaining why they could not stop checking their screens. (3) The problem was not that these students disliked reading; it was that the library had built a room for attention and then left the loudest distraction at the door. (4) When the branch began requiring phones to be checked into a locked cabinet during the hour, attendance dropped for two weeks and then doubled. (5) The change was not a punishment, as some students first assumed, but a permission slip: for sixty minutes, no one could expect an answer. (6) In that small silence, a ninth grader named Amara finished her first novel since sixth grade; a retired bus driver named Mr. Alvarez began a mystery series he now discusses with her every week. (7) A library cannot force anyone to love books, nor should it try. (8) It can, however, protect the conditions in which reading becomes possible: a chair, a lamp, and a stretch of time that no notification is allowed to split. (9) Yet the library should not turn every hour into a phone-free zone. (10) Patrons need access to job listings, online tutoring, and family calls, and a rule that ignores those needs would turn a helpful experiment into a lecture. (11) The reading hour works best as an invitation rather than a requirement. (12) On Thursday afternoons, the Eastside Branch is not quieter because it has banished technology; it is quieter because it has made room for one thing at a time.
questions.q: In sentence (5), the phrase “a permission slip” primarily conveys which idea about the phone-free hour?
options: It suggests that the policy is only temporary.
It makes the hour feel like an official school event.
It shows that students must ask permission to read.
It gives students relief from the expectation of immediate responses.
questions.explanation: The colon after “permission slip” explains the relief: for sixty minutes, no one can expect an answer. The phrase captures release from social pressure, not bureaucratic approval, transience, or permission to read.

the library’s rejection of all digital services.
a nostalgic preference for print books over screens.
questions.explanation: The construction sets aside a false reason—banishing technology—to identify the real cause: room for one thing at a time. It does not claim strict enforcement, reject digital services, or merely prefer print books.

options: criticize patrons who use phones instead of reading.
argue that the phone-free hour should be required all week.
propose replacing the reading hour with computer classes.
acknowledge legitimate reasons patrons rely on library technology.
questions.explanation: The list supports the concession that phones serve important needs and that a total ban would be unfair. It does not replace or condemn technology use, nor does it support a broader mandatory ban.

questions.q: The writer’s line of reasoning ultimately supports which recommendation about the reading hour?
options: Offer it as an optional program rather than a mandatory policy.
Extend it to every hour the library is open.
Require all patrons to surrender their phones at all times.
Cancel it because attendance first dropped.
questions.explanation: Sentence (11) states the recommendation after the concession in sentences (9) and (10): the hour works as an invitation. The earlier attendance drop is temporary and reversed, and the passage explicitly warns against a universal phone-free policy.

questions.q: The writer suspects that sentence (3) will confuse readers. Which replacement best makes the intended contrast clear?
options: The students disliked reading less than they disliked the library, which had built a room for attention.
The problem was not the students’ dislike of reading but the library’s distraction from the loud room.
The students did not dislike reading; the library had simply made room for phones in a space meant for concentration.
The library had built a room for attention, so the loudest distraction at the door was not the students’ dislike of reading.
questions.explanation: The original claims that the issue is not students’ attitude toward reading but a distracting environment. The correct replacement states that contrast directly. The alternatives confuse what is distracting, shift the comparison to students’ dislike of the library, or become garbled about where the distraction is.

questions.q: A student is revising the following sentence for a letter to the city council: “The new crosswalk will help students walk to school because they are often worried about traffic.” Which revision best clarifies the cause-and-effect relationship?
options: The new crosswalk will help students, often worried about traffic, walk to school.
Because students are often worried about traffic, the new crosswalk will help them walk to school.
Often worried about traffic, the new crosswalk will help students walk to school.
The new crosswalk will help students walk to school, and they are often worried about traffic.
questions.explanation: The correct revision uses a causal subordinate clause to connect students’ concern about traffic directly to the crosswalk’s benefit. The alternatives present the ideas as unrelated, attach the worry to the crosswalk itself, or leave the causal link only implied.

questions.q: A student is editing this sentence for a scholarship application: “The reason why I volunteer at the food pantry is because I want to help families who do not have enough food.” Which revision is clearest and most concise?
options: I volunteer at the food pantry because I want to help families who do not have enough food.
The reason I volunteer at the food pantry is that I want to help families who do not have enough food.
I volunteer at the food pantry because families who do not have enough food are who I want to help.
The reason why I volunteer at the food pantry is I want to help families with not enough food.
questions.explanation: The correct revision removes the redundant “reason why . . . is because” construction while keeping the causal meaning. The alternatives retain wordiness, invert the emphasis awkwardly, or introduce an ungrammatical phrase.

questions.topic: Style: word choice, syntax and tone
questions.q: A student wants the following sentence from an editorial to have a firm but respectful tone: “Drivers who oppose bike lanes are clinging to a fossil-fueled fantasy.” Which replacement for the quoted phrase best achieves that goal?
options: have not yet accounted for the long-term costs of car dependence.
refuse to join the modern city.
are stuck in a childish dream.
are blind to the obvious future.
questions.explanation: The correct phrase challenges the opposing view while framing it as an unfinished consideration of costs, which is firm and respectful. The other options insult opponents as blind, childish, or stubborn.

questions.topic: Rhetorical situation: audience, purpose and context
questions.q: A student is writing a proposal to the school board to create a small meditation room. The student knows that several board members are concerned about cost. Which opening sentence best addresses that concern while introducing the proposal?
options: A quiet room can be created in the unused conference space for less than the cost of one vending machine.
Many schools have meditation rooms, and ours should have one too.
Although some board members may not understand meditation, they should support this proposal.
Students are stressed, and meditation is a proven way to reduce stress.
questions.explanation: The correct opening acknowledges cost by providing a concrete low-expense solution in existing space. The other options ignore the board’s cost concern, rely on peer pressure, or sound condescending.

questions.q: A student is writing an essay arguing that high-school start times should be moved later. Which sentence would best serve as the thesis?
options: Many students are tired in the morning, and school start times are a complicated issue.
Some districts have changed their start times, but others have not.
According to sleep researchers, adolescents naturally stay up later and need more sleep.
Moving high school start times to 8:45 a.m. would improve students’ health and academic performance without disrupting most after-school activities.
questions.explanation: A thesis should present a precise, arguable claim that previews the line of reasoning. The correct sentence gives a specific change and two benefits while addressing disruption. The alternatives announce a topic, offer evidence, or describe disagreement rather than state the essay’s central argument.

questions.passage: (1) When Cedar Ridge opened its first bus rapid transit line two years ago, drivers predicted that removing a car lane from Crosstown Avenue would turn a ten-minute trip into a morning-long ordeal. (2) Instead, the city’s traffic engineers found that average car travel times along the corridor fell by nearly a minute, even as bus ridership doubled. (3) The lesson is not that buses are magic; it is that a street designed for every vehicle to move quickly often moves almost no one efficiently. (4) Before the redesign, the avenue carried four narrow lanes, no protected space for cyclists, and bus stops that consisted of a sign and a patch of broken concrete. (5) Riders waited in the rain beside diesel fumes, and drivers changed lanes every few seconds to escape slow-moving delivery trucks. (6) The new configuration gives buses a dedicated lane, shortens crosswalk distances, and adds trees between the sidewalk and traffic. (7) Some store owners worried that fewer parking spaces would drive customers away, so the city tracked receipts in the district for six months before and after construction. (8) Sales at shops within two blocks of the route rose slightly, while vacancies declined for the first time since the recession. (9) None of this means the project is beyond criticism. (10) Construction disrupted businesses for a year, and residents in the western neighborhoods still lack a direct connection to the line. (11) Yet the debate has shifted from whether to make room for buses to how far the network should extend. (12) A city that once measured progress by how fast a car could cross downtown now measures it by how many people can arrive without needing one.
questions.q: Which of the following best describes the function of sentence (9) in the passage?
options: It introduces a concession that qualifies the passage’s largely favorable account before specific drawbacks are acknowledged.
It reverses the passage’s argument by claiming that the transit project produced no measurable benefits.
It signals that sentence (10) will explain why the bus line should be discontinued.
It restates the financial evidence in sentences (7) and (8) as the project’s central purpose.
questions.explanation: Sentence (9) pivots from evidence of benefits to limitations, preparing readers for the drawbacks in sentence (10). It does not reverse the argument or call for ending the project; it balances the favorable account with a concession.

questions.q: Which claim is best supported by the details in sentences (7) and (8)?
options: Most store owners quickly became enthusiastic supporters of the bus-lane redesign.
The bus-lane redesign did not appear to harm nearby businesses, despite initial concerns.
Construction caused more economic damage than the completed project repaired.
The redesign eliminated commercial vacancies throughout Cedar Ridge.
questions.explanation: Sentences (7) and (8) describe store owners’ worries, the city’s tracking of receipts, a slight rise in sales, and a decline in vacancies near the route. Together these details support the limited claim that nearby businesses were not visibly harmed, not the sweeping claims about universal enthusiasm or citywide effects.

provide statistical proof that the bus lane initially made car trips much longer.

mock drivers for being unable to estimate travel time accurately.
questions.explanation: The phrase is a hyperbolic prediction attributed to drivers, setting up the contrast with the data in sentence (2). It expresses alarm and anticipated disruption, but it is not statistical proof that the prediction came true.

questions.q: The writer wants to revise sentence (11) to make its connection to the passage’s main claim clearer. Which revision best accomplishes that goal?
options: Yet the debate has changed, and many people now argue about buses.
Yet the debate has shifted from whether to make room for buses to how far the network should extend, which is a common issue in growing cities.
Yet the evidence has shifted the debate: the question is no longer whether buses deserve space on Crosstown Avenue but how far the network should extend.
Yet the debate has shifted; the network should extend farther.
questions.explanation: The revision explicitly connects the changed debate to the evidence the passage has presented and frames the remaining issue as the scope of the network. The other options are vague, add a generic aside, or state an unsupported recommendation.

options: create a nostalgic portrait of the avenue before construction.

questions.q: A student is revising the following sentence for clarity in a proposal to the school board: 'After speaking with students, the proposal to extend library hours was revised by the principal.' Which revision best improves clarity and coherence?
options: After speaking with students, revisions were made to the proposal to extend library hours by the principal.
The proposal to extend library hours, after speaking with students, was revised by the principal.
Speaking with students, the proposal to extend library hours was revised by the principal.
After speaking with students, the principal revised the proposal to extend library hours.
questions.explanation: The original sentence contains a dangling modifier: it suggests the proposal, not the principal, spoke with students. The clear revision makes the principal the subject of the opening modifier, while the other options keep or create the same confusion.

questions.topic: Style: word choice, syntax and tone
questions.q: Read the following sentence: 'The school garden was not merely a patch of tomatoes; it was a lesson in patience written in rows of green.' The syntax and figurative language in the sentence primarily serve to
options: provide a factual comparison between tomatoes and other vegetables.
shift the reader from a literal description of the garden to a broader interpretation of its value.
correct an earlier overstatement about the garden’s size.
create a humorous tone by mocking school gardening clubs.
questions.explanation: The construction not merely . . . it was reinterprets the garden, moving from physical tomatoes to a metaphor about patience and learning. The phrasing is reflective rather than factual, corrective, or mocking.

questions.q: A student is drafting a paragraph arguing that high school should start later. The paragraph begins with this sentence: 'Teenagers’ sleep patterns shift later during adolescence, making early start times especially difficult.' Which sentence would best follow to develop the argument logically?
options: So when high schools begin classes before 8 a.m., many students are asked to learn while their bodies are still signaling that they need sleep.
Many adults also remember having to wake up early for school.
Therefore, all schools should begin at exactly 9 a.m. every day.
In contrast, elementary school students often wake up early and are ready to learn.
questions.explanation: The sentence about adolescent sleep patterns logically leads to the consequence of early high school start times. The other options shift to a different age group, make an overly rigid recommendation, or offer an irrelevant personal memory.

questions.q: A student is writing an editorial arguing that the city should convert an abandoned rail line into a pedestrian and bicycle trail. Which claim would best be supported by evidence that nearby property values rose after a similar trail opened in another city?
options: The abandoned rail line is unsafe for pedestrians.
A rail-to-trail conversion can contribute to neighborhood economic vitality.
Most residents prefer biking to driving.
The trail will eliminate all traffic congestion downtown.
questions.explanation: Evidence about rising property values supports a measured claim about possible economic benefits. It does not support sweeping claims about eliminating traffic, proving most residents’ travel preferences, or describing the abandoned rail line as unsafe.

questions.topic: Rhetorical situation: audience, purpose and context
questions.passage: (1) In the winter of 1881, a small steam schooner left the Columbia River with barrels of salted salmon packed in spruce boxes. (2) Its destination was Honolulu, where merchants had begun advertising Columbia River fish as a cheap food for sugar-plantation workers. (3) At first glance, this trade seems like a simple exchange of one region's surplus for another's cash. (4) Yet the ledgers of the Astoria packers and the Honolulu grocers tell a more complicated story. (5) The salmon did not travel alone; it carried with it assumptions about taste, labor, and freshness that changed on both sides of the Pacific. (6) Honolulu buyers, for example, initially rejected the first shipments because the fish was too salty for local cooking. (7) Rather than abandon the market, Columbia River packers reduced the salt and began packing the fish in smaller casks suited to plantation kitchens. (8) Meanwhile, Hawaiian merchants used the new product to press plantation owners for better wholesale terms, arguing that a dependable imported protein could weaken the price of local fish. (9) These negotiations did not make the trade equal; the packers kept most of the profit, and the plantation workers who ate the fish had little say in its quality. (10) Still, the exchange reshaped both economies. (11) Columbia River canneries added winter shifts, and Honolulu markets developed new distribution routes along the waterfront. (12) The trade's importance, then, lay less in the barrels themselves than in the habits and relationships the barrels made possible. (13) When historians describe the Pacific Northwest's early export economy, they should treat the Hawaiian salmon trade not as a footnote but as a workshop where modern Pacific commerce was tested.
questions.q: The passage is most likely written for which audience?
options: Hawaiian plantation workers organizing for better wages and food quality
Columbia River cannery owners seeking instructions for reducing salt in their barrels
Readers of a regional history journal who are interested in how early Pacific trade shaped local economies
Elementary school students learning the basic steps of canning fish
questions.explanation: The passage uses historical evidence and an argument about how historians should interpret the trade, so it addresses readers of a regional history journal. It is not a recipe for canning, a set of instructions for cannery owners, or an organizing appeal to plantation workers.

options: Honolulu buyers rejected Columbia River fish at first because it was too salty for local cooking.
The salmon trade was unequal because packers kept most of the profits and workers had little say.
The Hawaiian salmon trade should be treated as a significant testing ground for modern Pacific commerce rather than a minor historical detail.
Columbia River canneries added winter shifts and Honolulu markets developed new waterfront routes.
questions.explanation: Sentence (13) explicitly argues that historians should treat the Hawaiian salmon trade as a workshop where modern Pacific commerce was tested, not as a footnote. The other choices are a supporting detail, a concession, or evidence about economic effects rather than the passage's main claim.

questions.passage: (1) In the winter of 1881, a small steam schooner left the Columbia River with barrels of salted salmon packed in spruce boxes. (2) Its destination was Honolulu, where merchants had begun advertising Columbia River fish as a cheap food for sugar-plantation workers. (3) At first glance, this trade seems like a simple exchange of one region's surplus for another's cash. (4) Yet the ledgers of the Astoria packers and the Honolulu grocers tell a more complicated story. (5) The salmon did not travel alone; it carried with it assumptions about taste, labor, and freshness that changed on both sides of the Pacific. (6) Honolulu buyers, for example, initially rejected the first shipments because the fish was too salty for local cooking. (7) Rather than abandon the market, Columbia River packers reduced the salt and began packing the fish in smaller casks suited to plantation kitchens. (8) Meanwhile, Hawaiian merchants used the new product to press plantation owners for better wholesale terms, arguing that a dependable imported protein could weaken the price of local fish. (9) These negotiations did not make the trade equal; the packers kept most of the profit, and the plantation workers who ate the fish had little say in its quality. (10) Still, the exchange reshaped both economies. (11) Columbia River canneries added winter shifts, and Honolulu markets developed new distribution routes along the waterfront. (12) The trade's importance, then, lay less in the barrels themselves than in the habits and relationships the barrels made possible. (13) When historians describe the Pacific Northwest's early export economy, they should treat the Hawaiian salmon trade not as a footnote but as a workshop where modern Pacific commerce was tested.
questions.q: Which best describes the function of sentences (6)-(8) in the passage?
options: They shift from historical analysis to a personal narrative about a Honolulu cook.
They state the passage's main claim and then list evidence that will appear in later sentences.
They argue that the trade had no lasting effect on either region.
They present specific adjustments and negotiations that support the idea that the trade changed practices and assumptions on both sides.
questions.explanation: These sentences show Honolulu buyers resisting the fish and Columbia River packers and Hawaiian merchants adjusting practices and negotiating terms. They therefore support the passage's larger claim that the trade changed assumptions and practices on both sides of the Pacific.

questions.q: Which detail from the passage most directly supports the claim that the trade changed practices in the Pacific Northwest?
options: Columbia River canneries added winter shifts.
Honolulu buyers initially rejected the fish as too salty.
Plantation workers had little say in fish quality.
Hawaiian merchants sought better wholesale terms.
questions.explanation: The added winter shifts show that Columbia River canneries altered their production schedule because of the trade. The other details describe Honolulu's responses, a limitation of the trade, or inequality rather than a change in Pacific Northwest practices.

questions.q: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence (11) to strengthen the argument that the trade had lasting effects beyond salmon. Which addition best achieves that purpose?
options: The trade was unequal because packers kept most of the profits.
Salted salmon was often packed in spruce boxes before shipment.
Within a decade, several Honolulu firms that had handled salmon were importing California fruit and Japanese rice along the same waterfront routes.
Plantation workers had little say in the quality of the fish they ate.
questions.explanation: The sentence shows that firms and routes connected to the salmon trade later carried different goods, demonstrating a lasting commercial impact beyond salmon. The other proposed additions merely restate packing details, emphasize inequality, or note workers' limited influence without showing long-term effects.

questions.topic: Rhetorical situation: audience, purpose and context
questions.q: Maya Chen is writing a letter to the editor of her local newspaper urging residents to support a new public library branch. Which of the following best describes the most important feature of the rhetorical situation for her letter?
options: Her context is a private journal, so she can assume readers already know the proposal's details.
Her purpose is to entertain readers with a humorous story about her own study habits.
Her audience consists mainly of library architects, so she should use technical terms about building design.
Her audience consists of community members who may be undecided and busy, so she should emphasize shared benefits and respond to likely concerns about cost.
questions.explanation: A letter to the editor is a public argument aimed at a broad, possibly undecided audience, so the writer should stress shared benefits and answer concerns about cost. Technical building terms, a humorous personal story, or private journal assumptions would not fit that rhetorical situation as well.

questions.q: A student is drafting an editorial arguing that the city should extend library hours during final exams. Which thesis best establishes a clear line of reasoning?
options: Extending library hours during final exams would help students who lack quiet study space, reduce crowding at the central branch, and support working students who study late.
Extending library hours is a topic that deserves careful consideration by city officials.
The library is an important place, and final exams are stressful for many students.
Many students have different opinions about the library and its hours.
questions.explanation: The thesis states a clear position and lists three specific reasons—quiet study space, crowding, and working students—that can organize the editorial. The other choices merely announce the topic or note that opinions vary.

questions.q: A student's paragraph begins: 'Critics of later school start times point to transportation costs. However, a district study found that adjusting bus routes would add only 2 percent to the transportation budget. In addition, later starts have improved attendance in neighboring districts.' Which best explains the function of the sentence beginning 'However'?
options: It introduces the paragraph's main claim by dismissing all opposing views.
It shifts the paragraph from transportation to an unrelated topic.
It provides a personal anecdote to illustrate the costs.
It concedes a counterargument before presenting evidence that limits its force.
questions.explanation: The sentence beginning 'However' acknowledges critics' transportation-cost objection and then uses a district study to lessen its force before adding further evidence. It does not dismiss all opposing views, offer an anecdote, or change to an unrelated topic.

questions.q: A student is drafting a paragraph arguing that the city should add shade to bus stops. Which claim is best supported by this evidence: 'A 2023 city survey found that 64 percent of bus riders without shade at their stops said they would ride more often in summer if shade were available'?
options: Most residents avoid buses in every season.
Adding shade at bus stops could increase summer ridership.
Bus riders prefer shade to lower fares.
Shade is the only way to improve public transportation.
questions.explanation: The survey directly links available shade to riders' stated willingness to ride more often in summer, so it supports the moderate claim that shade could increase summer ridership. It does not support claims about being the only solution, year-round avoidance, or preference over fares.

questions.q: A student is writing an argument that the city should extend library hours to serve working residents. Which source would provide the most relevant evidence?
options: A national blog post about the history of libraries
A city library system report comparing attendance and after-work use before and after a pilot program with later evening hours
A survey of nearby towns' museum hours
An opinion essay by a novelist who writes in cafes
questions.explanation: A local report comparing use before and after later hours directly addresses whether extended hours would serve working residents in the city. A general history blog, a novelist's opinion essay, and a survey of museum hours are far less relevant to that claim.

questions.topic: Style: word choice, syntax and tone
questions.passage: (1) In the third summer of the drought, the city of Red Mesa finally did what hydrologists had urged for years: it began paying residents to replace thirsty lawns with gravel and native brush. (2) The rebate checks made headlines, and water use dipped by eleven percent in a single season. (3) But a rebate is a starting gun, not a finish line. (4) The deeper lesson of Red Mesa is that conservation succeeds only when the city treats every rooftop, parking lot, and alley as part of its reservoir. (5) Rain that falls on a shingled roof and runs into a storm drain is not excess; it is supply that has been misplaced. (6) In older neighborhoods, narrow curbs and cracked sidewalks guide storm water toward the river, where it is lost to the city and, too often, carries motor oil into the ecosystem. (7) By installing rain gardens at bus stops and cutting shallow channels along schoolyards, Red Mesa could slow that runoff, allowing it to soak into the soil and recharge the wells that residents depend on. (8) These projects are less glamorous than a check in the mail, but they are also less vulnerable to a budget cycle. (9) A lawn rebate expires; a rain garden does not. (10) The city's next water plan should therefore pair its rebate program with a modest public-works initiative: one rain garden for every new block of asphalt the city repaves. (11) The cost would be small compared with the price of importing water from distant farms, a measure Red Mesa has already considered twice. (12) If residents can see rain as a neighbor rather than a nuisance, they will build a water supply that does not vanish when dry skies return.
questions.q: In sentence (3), the comparison of a rebate to “a starting gun, not a finish line” mainly conveys the writer’s view that the rebate program
options: has been designed primarily to attract media attention rather than conserve water
marks a promising beginning but cannot by itself complete the city’s conservation effort
is less effective than the rain gardens that the writer proposes later
has already resolved Red Mesa’s most urgent water shortage
questions.explanation: The metaphor contrasts the start of a race with its finish, so it presents the rebate as an initial step rather than a complete solution. The passage later supports this by arguing for additional rain gardens and channels. The mention of headlines does not imply the program was merely publicity, and the passage does not claim the shortage is already resolved.

questions.q: To clarify the link between the proposed projects and the contaminated runoff described in sentence (6), which change to sentence (7) would be most effective?
options: By installing rain gardens at bus stops and cutting shallow channels along schoolyards, Red Mesa could slow that runoff; the city's wells depend on residents.

By installing rain gardens at bus stops and cutting shallow channels along schoolyards, Red Mesa could slow the storm water’s rush toward the river, allowing it to soak into the soil and recharge the wells that residents depend on.
By installing rain gardens at bus stops, Red Mesa could cut shallow channels along schoolyards, allowing that runoff to soak into the soil and recharge the wells that residents depend on.
By installing rain gardens at bus stops and cutting shallow channels along schoolyards, Red Mesa could slow that runoff, which is why motor oil often reaches the ecosystem.
questions.explanation: The best revision replaces the vague “that runoff” with “the storm water’s rush toward the river,” directly connecting the projects to the runoff problem described in sentence (6). It also keeps the causal chain of slowing water so it can soak in and recharge wells. The option about motor oil reverses the logic, while the others confuse the sequence of actions or produce an unclear final clause.

questions.q: Which replacement for sentence (12) would best emphasize a long-term practical benefit while retaining the essay’s sympathetic, reflective tone?
options: If residents can see rain as a neighbor rather than a nuisance, they will finally stop complaining about cloudy days.
Residents must stop treating rain as a nuisance and start treating it as a neighbor; otherwise, the city will fail.
If residents can see rain as a neighbor rather than a nuisance, they will build a water supply that remains dependable through dry seasons.
If residents can see rain as a neighbor rather than a nuisance, they will understand why the city’s rebate checks made headlines.
questions.explanation: The revision keeps the neighbor/nuisance metaphor while making the benefit concrete and future-oriented: a dependable supply through dry seasons. It thus preserves the reflective tone and strengthens the practical case. The complaining version narrows the focus and sounds dismissive, the failure version becomes alarmist, and the headlines version returns to an earlier minor detail.

questions.q: The writer’s line of reasoning in sentences (3)-(5) moves from
options: qualifying the success of a popular program to introducing a broader principle about how water should be managed
criticizing hydrologists’ predictions to defending the rebate checks
describing a problem in older neighborhoods to proposing a specific public-works budget
contrasting city officials with residents to emphasizing the importance of lawns
questions.explanation: Sentence (3) concedes that the rebate program is a start, and sentences (4)-(5) expand into a general claim that the city must treat rooftops, lots, and alleys as reservoir space. That is a movement from qualified praise of a specific program to a broader management principle. The other descriptions refer to later parts of the passage or misread the sequence as criticism of hydrologists or emphasis on lawns.

questions.q: Given the passage’s context as an opinion piece for Red Mesa residents, the reference in sentence (11) to “importing water from distant farms” most likely serves to
options: argue that residents should oppose all public-works spending
provide statistical evidence that the rebate program saved eleven percent
show that farms outside Red Mesa are responsible for the city’s drought
present the rain-garden proposal as a more practical local alternative to a costly regional measure
questions.explanation: The cost comparison makes the rain-garden plan appear modest and local, especially beside the repeatedly considered option of importing water. This supports the writer’s purpose of persuading residents to favor the infrastructure proposal. The sentence does not blame farms for the drought, reject all public works, or provide evidence about the eleven-percent figure.

questions.topic: Style: word choice, syntax and tone
questions.q: A student’s draft sentence reads: “The river’s recovery has been patient, uneven, and, in places, stubbornly incomplete.” For a feature article on a wildlife refuge, the word “stubbornly” mainly helps the student
options: criticize volunteers for refusing to finish their work
create a playful contrast between nature and human stubbornness
suggest that the river is deliberately resisting conservation efforts
emphasize that progress persists despite lingering problems, with a tone of qualified hope
questions.explanation: “Stubbornly incomplete” suggests that the recovery has persisted even where it remains imperfect, which supports a cautious hope rather than a clean success. The word personifies the recovery slightly but does not mean the river is deliberately resisting or that volunteers are at fault. It also does not create a light or playful contrast with human stubbornness.

questions.q: Which version of the following sentence for a neighborhood newsletter makes the city’s purpose clearest by connecting it directly to the rain barrels? “The new rain barrels that residents can buy at a discount collect water from downspouts, and the city hopes they will reduce storm-water runoff.”
options: Residents can buy new rain barrels at a discount; storm-water runoff is reduced by the city’s hope.
The new rain barrels collect water from downspouts, and residents can buy them at a discount, and the city hopes they will reduce storm-water runoff.
The city hopes that new discount rain barrels, which residents can attach to downspouts, will reduce storm-water runoff.
Because the new rain barrels collect water from downspouts, residents can buy them at a discount, reducing storm-water runoff.
questions.explanation: The revision makes the city’s hope the main clause and attaches the downspout detail directly to the rain barrels, so the purpose and mechanism are clear. The stringy version keeps the two ideas loosely coordinated, the passive “city’s hope” version is vague, and the causal version suggests residents receive discounts because the barrels collect water.

questions.topic: Rhetorical situation: audience, purpose and context
questions.q: A student is preparing a brief speech for a campus Earth Day assembly. The audience includes students and teachers who already support recycling but are unfamiliar with the school’s new wildlife garden. The student wants to recruit volunteers. Which opening sentence best fits this rhetorical situation?
options: Scientists classify butterflies and birds according to kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species.
Most of us already separate cans from paper, so here is a chance to take the next step: spend one lunch hour helping the new wildlife garden attract butterflies and birds.
If you do not volunteer for the wildlife garden, you clearly do not care about the planet.
Recycling is a controversial issue that has divided our school for decades.
questions.explanation: The opening acknowledges the audience’s existing recycling habits and then offers a concrete, low-commitment action tied to Earth Day and the new garden. It thereby recruits volunteers without seeming to lecture people who already support environmental work. The other openings are inaccurate, overly technical, or accusatory for this audience and purpose.

questions.q: A student has gathered these notes for an op-ed about a campus water-bottle ban: single-use bottles make up nearly one-third of the campus waste stream; refill stations have cut bottle use in two dorms by 20 percent; some students with disabilities rely on bottled water during heat waves. Which thesis best organizes these notes into a defensible argument?
options: Single-use water bottles are the most serious environmental problem facing the campus today.
Because two dorms reduced bottle use by 20 percent, every student should be required to use a refill station.
The campus should ban single-use water bottles while preserving an exemption and accessible refill options for students who need them.
Students who rely on bottled water during heat waves should not be allowed to participate in the ban discussion.
questions.explanation: The best thesis takes a clear position while accommodating the evidence that some students need bottled water and that refill access matters. It can organize both the waste-reduction data and the concern about accessibility. The other statements overstate the problem, overgeneralize from a limited result, or exclude affected students rather than advancing a defensible policy.

questions.q: A student is drafting an argument for a county wildlife corridor. The draft explains that deer-vehicle collisions have increased, that underpasses in a neighboring county reduced such collisions by 40 percent, and that the underpasses cost $2 million. Which sentence would best conclude the paragraph by turning the evidence into a qualified recommendation?
options: Given the demonstrated safety benefits, the county should fund a corridor with underpasses while seeking state grants to offset the cost.
Wildlife corridors are interesting, but our county has many other issues to consider.
The neighboring county spent $2 million on underpasses, which proves that all infrastructure projects are too expensive.
Deer-vehicle collisions are increasing, so the county must immediately ban all cars at night.
questions.explanation: The recommendation follows from the evidence: collisions are a problem, underpasses succeeded elsewhere, and cost is a real constraint, so the county should pursue the corridor while seeking funding support. This qualified conclusion uses all the notes without overreacting or dismissing the cost. The other sentences either propose an extreme ban, misuse the cost figure, or avoid making a recommendation.

questions.passage:
(1) Our farm's harvest calendar used to begin with a cloud of dust.
(2) My grandfather would hook the chisel plow to the tractor, and by noon the field would look combed and clean.
(3) Dust hung over the road for hours, and every neighbor nodded as if we had done something important.
(4) Clean, we now know, was the wrong word.
(5) Each pass broke the soil into fine particles that rain could carry away, along with the fertilizer we had paid for.
(6) After three springs of watching muddy water leave the lower field, my parents agreed to try a cover crop of cereal rye.
(7) The first harvest after planting rye did not look like progress.
(8) The combine sometimes clogged, and the field seemed shaggy next to our neighbor's.
(9) But by October, water stood in our neighbor's furrows while our rows soaked it up like a sponge.
(10) A soil test also showed that organic matter on the rye field had risen from 2.3 percent to 2.8 percent in two years.
(11) That half-percentage point may sound small, but it means more carbon and water held in the ground.
(12) For our family, the lesson is not that every old method is wrong.
(13) It is that a tidy field and a healthy field are not always the same thing.
(14) A harvest is not just what the combine collects; it is also what the soil keeps.
questions.q: The detail about neighbors nodding in sentence (3) primarily serves to
options: prove that dust from the field improved relations among neighboring farms
show that the grandfather's plowing method was widely admired, which makes the passage's later reevaluation of that method more significant
provide statistical evidence that the old method increased crop yields
suggest that the family first planted rye because of pressure from neighbors
questions.explanation: The nodding neighbors establish that the dusty plowing was once viewed as an accomplishment, so the family's later shift away from it gains significance. The sentence offers social approval, not proof of improved relations, pressure from neighbors, or statistical evidence about yields.

questions.q: Taken together, sentences (9) and (10) provide the strongest support for which conclusion?
options: The soil test was taken before the rye was planted.
The rye field produced a larger harvest than the neighbor's field.
The neighbor's field had lower organic matter because it lacked fertilizer.
The rye field retained more water and showed a measurable increase in soil organic matter.
questions.explanation: Sentence (9) contrasts water standing in the neighbor's furrows with the rye rows soaking up water, and sentence (10) reports soil organic matter rising from 2.3 to 2.8 percent. Nothing in those sentences supports a claim about harvest size, the timing of the soil test, or fertilizer use.

(5) Each pass broke the soil into fine particles that rain could carry away, along with the fertilizer we had paid for.
(6) After three springs of watching muddy water leave the lower field, my parents agreed to try a cover crop of cereal rye.
(7) The first harvest after planting rye did not look like progress.
(8) The combine sometimes clogged, and the field seemed shaggy next to our neighbor's.
(9) But by October, water stood in our neighbor's furrows while our rows soaked it up like a sponge.
(10) A soil test also showed that organic matter on the rye field had risen from 2.3 percent to 2.8 percent in two years.
(11) That half-percentage point may sound small, but it means more carbon and water held in the ground.
(12) For our family, the lesson is not that every old method is wrong.
(13) It is that a tidy field and a healthy field are not always the same thing.
(14) A harvest is not just what the combine collects; it is also what the soil keeps.
questions.q: In sentence (4), the phrase "Clean, we now know, was the wrong word" mainly creates a tone of
options: retrospective correction, as the writer reassesses a value once taken for granted
technical detachment, as the writer defines a soil term without judgment
amused nostalgia, as the writer fondly recalls a grandfather's habits
defensive anger, as the writer blames neighbors for misunderstanding the farm
questions.explanation: The phrase signals that the writer's understanding of "clean" has changed over time, giving the sentence a reflective, corrective tone. It does not sound amused, merely technical, or angry at neighbors.

questions.q: The writer wants to revise sentence (11) to make its connection to sentence (10) clearer. Which revision best accomplishes that goal?
options: The soil test's half-percentage point means more carbon and water, which are held in the ground.
A small percentage point means more carbon and water held in the ground.

questions.explanation: The correct revision keeps the reference to the half-percentage point and clarifies the contrast between its small appearance and its significance. The other revisions either weaken that contrast, drop the precise reference, or make the sentence vaguer.

questions.q: Which sentence most directly acknowledges a drawback of the family's switch to a cover crop?

questions.q: While drafting an argument that the city should convert an empty lot into a community garden, Maya has written this sentence: "The lot has sat unused for six years, collecting weeds and broken glass." Which sentence, if added next, would best advance her argument by linking this evidence to her claim?
options: Turning that neglected space into a garden would give nearby residents a safe, productive place to gather.
The city's parks department employs several full-time maintenance workers.
Weeds and broken glass can be found in vacant lots throughout the city.
Some empty lots are used for parking, which can also serve a community need.
questions.explanation: The correct addition explicitly connects the lot's neglect to the proposed garden's benefits. The other choices either introduce an unrelated comparison, offer irrelevant information, or generalize the problem without advancing the argument.
